title: Chips Up, Wires Down
headline: AI hardware lifted the Nasdaq-100 1.13% while AT&T and Netflix sank communication services and the 10-year held at 5.13%, a narrow tape that cost the model's value-tilted equity picks 48bp.
body:
### The day in one paragraph

Yesterday the troops carried the market; today the generals took the lead back. The S&P 500 rose 0.59% to 7,758 and the Nasdaq-100 1.13%, while the equal-weighted S&P 500 added 0.36% and the Russell 2000 only 0.16%. AI hardware did the lifting: Super Micro jumped 9.5% on a raised revenue guide, Nvidia gained 2.5% and the semiconductor fund 1.9%. The wires were cut on the other side, as AT&T fell 6.4% and Netflix 5.3%, dragging communication services down 1.1%. The 10-year Treasury yield edged up 1bp to 5.13% and the VIX eased 0.63 points to 16.7.

### Scoreboard

| Market | Close | Day | Year to date |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 | 7,758 | +0.59% | +13.3% |
| Nasdaq-100 | 29,823 | +1.13% | +18.1% |
| S&P 500 equal weight (RSP, price) | 216.64 | +0.36% | +13.1% |
| Russell 2000 | 2,781 | +0.16% | +12.1% |
| Developed ex-US (EFA, price) | 104.06 | +0.36% | +8.4% |
| Emerging markets (EEM, price) | 63.57 | +0.39% | +16.2% |
| 10-year Treasury | 5.13% | +1bp | +95bp |
| High yield (HYG, price) | 76.98 | +0.20% | −4.5% |
| WTI crude | $97.15 | −0.68% | +69.2% |
| Gold | $4,150 | +0.18% | −4.4% |
| Dollar index | 101.51 | −0.01% | +3.5% |
| Bitcoin | $84,760 | +2.19% | −3.1% |

*Futures, the dollar and bitcoin as of about 5:30pm ET.*

### What drove it

**Chips Up, Wires Down.** Technology rose 1.67% and was the day's best sector; Apple added 1.3%, Micron 2.0% and Broadcom 1.0%. Seven of eleven sectors gained. The losers were the defensive and the disappointed: communication services (−1.1%, Alphabet −1.6%), real estate (−0.7%), staples (−0.7%) and health care (−0.5%), which gave back a little of yesterday's run to a record.

**Beat, then sold.** AT&T earned $0.65 a share against $0.60 expected on revenue of $32.3bn against $31.7bn, and still lost 6.4%. Elevance crushed estimates ($6.99 vs $4.71) and fell 1.4%; Philip Morris beat by 6 cents and slipped 1.2%. Danaher was the exception, up 4.4% after earning $2.11 against $1.92. A beat buys nothing this season without a guide to match.

**Bonds hold the line at 5%.** The 2-year rose 2bp to 4.81% and the 10-year 1bp, leaving the 2s10s curve at 32bp. The 20-year auction cleared at 5.469%, against 5.42% at the prior sale. The 30-year mortgage rate dipped to 7.41% from 7.50% and applications still fell 5.3%, purchases 7.3%. Housing gets no relief at these levels.

**Oil splits in two.** The EIA reported a 3.1m-barrel crude draw against 0.8m expected and a 3.0m gasoline draw against 0.4m. WTI still slipped 0.7% to $97.15 while Brent rose 1.1% to $109.97, a $12.82 spread that keeps the pain offshore. Natural gas fell 5.8% to $2.79.

**After the bell.** Meta topped revenue estimates ($64.6bn vs $63.3bn), raised its AI spending plans, and traded about 3% higher; a lawsuit settlement charge cut reported earnings to $3.83 a share. Tesla earned $0.48 against $0.45 on revenue in line at $28.0bn and slipped about 2%. Lam Research beat narrowly and fell about 6%; IBM beat on both lines and eased about 1%; Texas Instruments ($2.62 vs $2.44) edged higher.

### The model's day

A narrow-leadership tape again went against the model's equity picks. The stocks-versus-bonds call, 67% equities against a 60% neutral, earned +3bp over a 60/40 mix as global stocks beat the Aggregate, and the fixed income tilts were flat against the Agg. Favored minus avoided sleeves lost 48bp: regional banks were unchanged, oil producers fell 0.5% and the UK 0.1%, while the avoided metals and mining sleeve rose 0.9%. Tesla's after-hours slip gives the consumer discretionary avoid a better start to tomorrow.

### Tomorrow

Jobless claims at 8:30am ET (200,000 expected, 199,000 prior) and the leading index at 10am (−0.1% expected). Earnings from Valero, Comcast, Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin, Union Pacific, Honeywell and American Airlines before the open; Newmont after the close.

title: Rockets Before the Reckoning
headline: Futures lean higher on SpaceX and Super Micro while oil nears $100, but Meta and Tesla after the close decide whether tech can retake the lead from yesterday's broad rally.
body:
### Overnight

Tech wants back in front. Nasdaq-100 futures are up 0.66% at 7am ET, S&P 500 futures 0.25% and Russell 2000 futures 0.15%; Dow futures add 0.10%. The lift comes from AI hardware: SpaceX is up about 10% before the open after earning $0.35 a share against $0.14 expected on $14.6 billion of revenue, and Super Micro is up 12% after raising its quarterly revenue guide to $18.5–19.5 billion from $14.5–15.5 billion. Netflix is the drag, down about 6% after revenue of $12.87 billion came in a hair under estimates.

Yesterday the S&P 500 rose 0.28% to 7,712.57 and the Dow 1.02% to 52,495.88, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.02%. The Russell 2000 gained 1.65%.

Oil is the cost of the rally. WTI is up about 1% to near $99 and Brent near $110 as Reuters reports Iran is drawing out talks with Washington ahead of the November 3 midterms. The 10-year yields 5.12%, flat on the close, and the 2-year 4.79%. The dollar index is little changed at 101.79, gold near $4,140 and bitcoin up 2.4% to about $83,400. The VIX sits at 17.3.

Overseas, the Nikkei rose 0.9% and the DAX is up 0.5%, while the Hang Seng fell 0.9% and Shanghai 0.6%.

### Today's calendar

| Time (ET) | Event | Consensus | Prior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7:00 | MBA mortgage applications | — | — |
| 10:30 | EIA crude inventories | — | — |
| 1:00 | $13 billion 20-year bond auction | — | — |

No Fed speakers: the committee is in its quiet period before the October 27–28 meeting, and futures price an 85% chance of no change.

Before the open, the beats are broad. **Elevance** earned $6.99 a share against $4.68 expected, **Thermo Fisher** $6.68 against $6.40 and **AT&T** $0.65 against $0.60, all with revenue ahead. **Wabtec** beat on earnings ($2.83 vs $2.73) and missed on revenue ($3.12 billion vs $3.20 billion).

After the close comes the main event: **Meta** (revenue expected at $63.3 billion), **Tesla** ($0.45 a share on $27.9 billion), **IBM** ($2.86), **Texas Instruments** ($2.42), **Lam Research** ($2.18).

### What would move the model

Tesla is the test for the dashboard's avoid on consumer discretionary, a sleeve at 23.3 times forward earnings. A miss on flat revenue would vindicate it; a beat with margin repair would make it the first call to revisit. Tonight's regional bank prints (Pinnacle, SouthState, Fulton, Texas Capital) check the top preference, regional banks at 1.2 times book. Oil near $100 keeps the oil producers' preference in the money; a large EIA build would be the first crack.

The stocks-vs-bonds call, 67% equities against a 60% neutral, rests on the 2s10s curve at 33bp against a 103bp median. A soft 20-year auction that steepens the long end would erode that edge. The risk signal stays high yield: spreads at 3.29% on Monday, and a move through 3.50% would have us trimming equity risk.

### Bottom line

We give the open 65% odds of holding its gains into the close, with Meta and Tesla setting tomorrow's tone. Own breadth, banks and producers; make megacap tech earn it tonight.

title: Equal Weight, Unequal Day
headline: The equal-weighted S&P 500 rose 1.15% and the Russell 2000 1.66% while the Nasdaq-100 slipped, as health care led a broad rally, housing data sank and the model's value-tilted equity picks won back 111bp.
body:
### The day in one paragraph

Yesterday the generals marched alone; today the troops did the work. The S&P 500 added 0.26% to 7,711 and the Nasdaq-100 slipped 0.13%, but the equal-weighted S&P 500 rose 1.15%, the Russell 2000 1.66% and the Dow 1.02%. Ten of eleven sectors gained; technology, down 0.28%, was the lone loser after a South Korean data-center IPO flop revived the AI-financing worry. Health care led with a 2.37% gain. Oil eased 0.7% on hopes of U.S.-Iran diplomacy, Treasuries rallied at the long end, and the VIX fell 1.13 points to 17.3.

### Scoreboard

| Market | Close | Day | Year to date |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 | 7,711 | +0.26% | +12.6% |
| Nasdaq-100 | 29,490 | −0.13% | +16.8% |

| Emerging markets (EEM, price) | 63.32 | +0.02% | +15.7% |
| 10-year Treasury | 5.12% | −3bp | +94bp |
| High yield (HYG, price) | 76.83 | −0.01% | −4.7% |

| Gold | $4,143 | −0.42% | −4.6% |
| Dollar index | 101.52 | −0.28% | +3.5% |
| Bitcoin | $82,817 | +1.19% | −5.4% |

*Futures, the dollar and bitcoin as of about 5pm ET.*

### What drove it

**Housing goes into the freezer.** Housing starts fell 5.2% in September to 1.221m against 1.30m expected; permits held at 1.40m, in line. Pending home sales dropped 7.3% on the month against a 0.5% dip expected and are down 11.3% from a year ago; Reuters puts the index at a record low. With mortgage rates near 7.5%, housing is the first casualty of a 5% 10-year.

**Bonds read it as growth news.** The 30-year yield fell 6bp to 5.42% and the 10-year 3bp to 5.12%, while the 2-year rose 2bp to 4.79% as the market holds on to a December hike. The 2s10s curve flattened 5bp to 33bp. The 10-year breakeven sat at 2.35%, so the long-end rally was real yields, and the bond proxies cashed in: real estate rose 1.70% and utilities 1.26%.

**Beats get paid, mostly.** Northrop Grumman earned $7.89 a share against $7.18 expected and rose 4.6%; 3M beat ($2.50 vs $2.38) and gained 5.8%; Hasbro earned $2.90 against $1.86 and jumped 11.2%. RTX beat by 48 cents and rose only 0.6%. GE Aerospace beat on earnings ($2.25 vs $2.01) and revenue ($14.1bn vs $12.9bn) and still fell 3.7%. GM matched estimates at $3.70, topped revenue at $50.0bn, then warned of a rocky 2027 and lost 6.8%. This season the guide sets the price.

**Health care catches a bid.** Eli Lilly rose 3.5%, Merck 3.3%, UnitedHealth 3.0% and Johnson & Johnson 2.2%; the sector fund touched a 52-week high.

**After the bell.** SpaceX earned $0.35 a share against $0.13 expected on revenue of $14.6bn against $12.9bn and traded about 5% higher. Netflix beat on earnings ($0.87 vs $0.82) with revenue in line and fell about 6%; Intuitive Surgical beat ($3.00 vs $2.65) and fell about 7%.

### The model's day

A clean sweep for the session. The stocks-versus-bonds call, at 67% equities, earned +2bp over a 60/40 mix, and the fixed income tilts added +2bp over the Agg. The equity picks won back 111bp of yesterday's 160bp loss: regional banks rose 2.0%, the UK 0.9% and oil producers 0.3%, while the avoided metals and mining (−1.0%) and aerospace and defense (−0.8%) sleeves fell. Consumer discretionary, also avoided, rose 0.9%. This is the tape the model is built for: breadth over concentration, cash flow over promises.

### Tomorrow

A quiet data day: EIA crude inventories (0.3m draw expected) and a 20-year bond auction. The earnings are not quiet: Meta, Tesla, IBM, AT&T, Elevance, Abbott, Thermo Fisher, SAP, Philip Morris, NextEra, Lam Research and Texas Instruments. Meta's capex guide is the one that decides whether today's rotation lasts.

title: Seoul Searching
headline: Nasdaq-100 futures are down 0.6% after a flopped Korean data-center IPO sank the KOSPI 3.7%, while beats at RTX, GE Aerospace and Northrop put the model's aerospace-and-defense avoid to the test.
body:
### Overnight

Monday's chip bounce did not survive the flight to Seoul. A flopped data-center IPO in South Korea sent the KOSPI down 3.7%, and the AI-financing worry is back on the US screen: Nasdaq-100 futures are down 0.6% and S&P 500 futures 0.2% at 7,720. Dow futures are flat and Russell 2000 futures off 0.1%. That gives back about half of Monday's 1.2% Nasdaq-100 gain; the S&P 500 closed up 0.4% at 7,691.

Asia was mostly red. The Nikkei fell 1.3% and the Hang Seng 1.3%; Shanghai eked out 0.1%. Europe is softer: the DAX is down 0.4%, the Euro Stoxx 50 0.5% and the FTSE 100 0.6%. German producer prices rose 6.7% from a year earlier against 5.3% expected and 4.6% prior, and the ZEW sentiment index slipped to 28.1 against 30.

Bonds are the morning's cushion. The 10-year Treasury yields 5.09%, 4bp lower overnight, and the 30-year 5.42%. Oil is not helping: WTI is up 1.6% to $100.13 and Brent 1.2% to $110.90. The dollar index eased 0.1% to 101.65, the yen firmed to 157.91, gold is down 0.6% at $4,134 and bitcoin 0.4% at $81,523.

### Today's calendar

| Time (ET) | Event | Consensus | Prior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8:30 | Housing starts, Sep | 1.30m | 1.275m |
| 8:30 | Building permits, Sep | 1.39m | 1.403m |
| 10:00 | Pending home sales, Sep (m/m) | −0.5% | +0.3% |
| 4:30pm | API crude inventories, week to Oct 16 | −1.3m bbl | −11.1m bbl |

No Fed speakers: the committee is in its quiet period before the October 27–28 meeting. No coupon auction today; $13 billion of 20-year bonds sell tomorrow (Treasury schedule, via Newsquawk).

The defense primes came out swinging before the open. **RTX** earned $2.26 a share against $1.78 expected, on revenue of $24.97 billion against $24.11 billion. **GE Aerospace** made $2.25 against $2.01, on $14.12 billion against $12.88 billion. **Northrop Grumman** made $7.89 against $7.18, with revenue of $11.12 billion a hair under the $11.14 billion estimate. **GM** earned $3.70 against $3.69 on $50.0 billion of revenue against $48.8 billion. **3M** ($2.50 vs $2.38) and **KeyCorp** ($0.51 vs $0.46) also beat. After the close: **Netflix** ($0.82 on $12.87 billion), **SpaceX**, **United Airlines** ($2.57), **Capital One** ($5.50), **Chubb** ($6.79) and **Intuitive Surgical** ($2.65).

### What would move the model

The cleanest test is one of the model's avoids. Aerospace & defense sits on the avoid list at 25.9 times forward earnings and 9% below its 200-day average, and RTX, GE Aerospace and Northrop all beat. If ITA rallies on the prints, the avoid costs the model; a fade would say 25.9 times already priced the beats. On the favored side, KeyCorp's beat is a modest plus for regional banks, and $100 oil supports the E&P overweight.

The stocks-versus-bonds call, 67% equities against a 60% neutral, rests on a flat curve: 2s10s at +38bp on Monday's close against a +103bp median. A weak starts number that rallies the 2-year would steepen it and thin that edge. High-yield spreads were 3.31% on Friday; a move through 3.50% is where we would trim equity risk.

### Bottom line

We give the Nasdaq 60% odds of closing lower today; the AI trade wants proof, and Netflix and SpaceX tonight are a sideshow before Meta tomorrow. Stay with breadth, banks and producers, and let the defense tape show whether the beats outrun a 25.9 multiple.

title: Chips Bounce, Bonds Balk
headline: The Nasdaq-100 rose 1.2% as chips rebounded, but the equal-weighted S&P 500 fell and the 10-year yield climbed 6bp to 5.15%, a narrow relief rally that cost the model's value-tilted equity picks 160bp.
body:
### The day in one paragraph

The generals came back to work. After last week's chip rout, the Nasdaq-100 rose 1.2% and the S&P 500 0.4% to 7,691, but the equal-weighted S&P 500 slipped 0.3%: a rebound carried by a handful of megacaps, with most of the index sitting it out. Bonds did not join the relief. The 10-year Treasury yield rose 6bp to 5.15%, utilities fell 2.0% and real estate 1.2%, the sectors that trade as bond proxies. The VIX eased 1.55 points to 18.4 as the scramble for hedges cooled ahead of the megacap earnings this week.

### Scoreboard

### What drove it

**Chips off the mat.** Last week's 10.5% fall in semiconductors left room for a bounce, and buyers took it. The VanEck semiconductor fund rose 1.6%, Micron 3.0%, Broadcom 1.8% and Nvidia 1.4%. Amazon led the megacaps with a 5.0% gain and Tesla added 3.8%. Technology (+1.4%) and consumer discretionary (+1.8%) were the only sectors up more than 0.1%; eight of eleven fell. The AI-financing worry goes to trial this week, when the spenders report.

**Rates rule the rest.** A 6bp rise in the 10-year with oil slipping 0.5% reads as supply and Fed risk: the 10-year breakeven held at 2.35%, investment grade credit (LQD) lost 0.5% on duration while high yield held flat. Talk of an October Fed hike is no longer fringe after last week's hot CPI and PPI. Utilities, real estate, financials (−0.8%, JPMorgan −1.8%) and staples (−0.5%) paid for it.

**Housing cracks first.** The NAHB builder index fell to 29 against 32 expected, the lowest since June 2012. With the 10-year above 5%, we expect tomorrow's starts and permits to disappoint rather than confirm a bottom.

**Steel surprise.** Cleveland-Cliffs earned $0.28 a share against $0.21 expected and jumped 16.3%, though revenue of $5.61bn missed the $5.69bn estimate.

### The model's day

A split decision. The stocks-versus-bonds call, at 67% equities against a 60% neutral, earned +4bp over a 60/40 mix as global stocks beat the Aggregate. The fixed income tilts added +1bp over the Agg. The equity picks had a rough session: favored minus avoided sleeves lost 160bp. Regional banks, oil producers and the UK all fell, while the avoided consumer discretionary sleeve rallied with Amazon and Tesla and metals and mining rose behind Cliffs. A beta bounce is the tape that punishes a value-and-cash-flow tilt; judge it on earnings weeks, not relief rallies.

### Tomorrow

Housing starts (1.31m expected, 1.275m prior) and permits (1.40m) at 8:30am ET, pending home sales at 10am. Earnings from GM, RTX, GE Aerospace, Netflix, Capital One, Northrop Grumman, 3M, Intuitive Surgical and United Airlines.

title: Chips Off the Floor
headline: Nasdaq futures are up 1.2% after the chip rout and China's 4.5% growth beat, and Fifth Third's earnings beat gives the model's regional-bank call its first test before Zions and Western Alliance report tonight.
body:
### Overnight

The buyers are back, at least for breakfast. Nasdaq-100 futures are up 1.2% after the index's worst week since June, and S&P 500 futures are up 0.5%. Russell 2000 futures add 0.4%; Dow futures slip 0.2%. Friday left plenty to recover: the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659 and semiconductors (SMH) another 3.4%.

The macro tape helps. China's third-quarter GDP grew 4.5% from a year earlier against 4.4% expected and 4.3% prior, with retail sales up 1.1% against 0.5% expected. Oil is easing after a Russia sanctions waiver: WTI is down 1.4% at $97.65, Brent 1.5% at $108.20. That takes some pressure off the long end. The 10-year yields 5.09%, flat on Friday's close, and the 2-year 4.74%. The dollar index is unchanged at 101.64, the yen weaker at 158.25 per dollar, gold flat at $4,185 and bitcoin up 0.6% to $82,467. The VIX has eased to 18.6 from 20.0.

Overseas is mixed. Korea's KOSPI rose 1.8% and Shanghai 0.4%, while the Nikkei fell 0.6%. In Europe, the DAX is down 0.6% and the energy-heavy FTSE 100 1.3% as Brent slips.

### Today's calendar

| Time (ET) | Event | Consensus | Prior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8:30 | Canada CPI, Sep (y/y) | 3.2% | 3.0% |
| 8:30 | Canada CPI-trim, Sep (y/y) | 1.9% | 1.9% |
| 10:00 | NAHB housing index, Oct | 32 | 32 |
| 10:30 | Bank of Canada Business Outlook Survey | — | — |
| 11:30 | 3-month bill auction | 4.009% | 4.085% |
| 11:30 | 6-month bill auction | — | 4.20% |

No Fed speakers: the October 27–28 meeting has the committee in its quiet period.

Earnings are a regional-bank show. Before the open, **Fifth Third** earned $1.13 a share against $0.83 expected, on revenue of $3.28 billion against $3.34 billion. **Cleveland-Cliffs** made $0.28 against $0.21, on $5.61 billion of revenue against $5.69 billion. After the close: **Steel Dynamics** ($5.48 expected on $6.43 billion), **W. R. Berkley** ($1.15), **Crown Holdings** ($2.26), **Zions** ($1.64), **Western Alliance** ($2.42) and **Wintrust** ($3.31).

### What would move the model

Regional banks are the dashboard's top equity preference, priced at 1.2 times book. Fifth Third's beat came with a revenue miss, so net interest income is the line to read tonight from Zions and Western Alliance. A second revenue shortfall would say the cheap valuation is earned.

The stocks-vs-bonds call, 67% equities against a 60% neutral, rests on valuation: the 2s10s curve at +35bp against a +103bp median leaves little term premium in bonds. A bull steepening led by the 2-year would erode that edge. The risk signal is credit. High-yield spreads sat at 3.23% on Thursday; a push through 3.50% would have us cutting equity risk.

### Bottom line

We would treat today's bounce as relief, and we give it 55% odds of holding into Meta on Wednesday. Own breadth and the banks, let chips prove themselves, and watch high yield more than the Nasdaq.

title: Capex on Trial, the Fed on Mute
headline: With the Fed in its quiet period, Meta's spending plan, the 20-year auction and $99 oil decide whether last week's tech rout spreads or stalls.
body:
### Setting the scene

The market walks into the week with a split personality. The S&P 500 fell 1.9% last week to 7,659, yet it is still up 11.9% for the year and only 2.4% below its 52-week high. The damage sat in the AI trade: the Nasdaq-100 lost 5.5% and semiconductors (SMH) 10.5%. The average stock barely noticed. Equal weight (RSP) rose 0.5% and consumer staples (XLP) 5.0%.

The macro inputs are not friendly. WTI closed Friday at $99.02, up 7.8% on the week and 72% this year; Brent finished at $109.86. The 10-year Treasury yields 5.09%, the 2-year 4.74%. The VIX jumped to 20.0 from 16.5 on Friday alone. And the Fed is out of the conversation: the October 27–28 meeting puts it in its pre-meeting quiet period from Saturday, October 17, so there are no Fed speakers on the calendar this week. Earnings, auctions and oil will do the talking.

### The big three questions

1. **Does AI capex still have a buyer?** Meta reports Wednesday with consensus at $6.58 a share on $63.3 billion of revenue; Tesla, the same day, at $0.45 on $27.9 billion. Lam Research and Texas Instruments also report Wednesday, after SMH's 10.5% drop. The beat matters less than next year's spending plan. A Meta capex guide that holds or rises says last week was digestion. A trim says the cycle is turning, and the Nasdaq-100 has further to fall.
2. **Will real money buy the long end at 5%-plus?** The 10-year fell 15bp last week while stocks sold off. Wednesday's 20-year auction last cleared at 5.42%; Thursday's 5-year TIPS at 1.955%. A sloppy 20-year tail would tell us the rally was short-covering.
3. **How far does $99 oil travel?** It shows up first abroad: UK CPI Wednesday (3.4% expected, 3.1% prior), Canada CPI Monday (3.2% expected, 3.0% prior) and Japan CPI late Thursday (2.3% expected, 1.9% prior). At home, Friday's flash PMIs (composite 57.6 expected, 58.4 prior) show whether costs are eating into activity.

### Day by day

| Day | Data and events | Earnings |
|---|---|---|
| Mon Oct 19 | China Q3 GDP (4.4% y/y expected, 4.3% prior), industrial production (5.4%, 5.2%), retail sales (0.5%, 0.4%); Canada CPI (3.2%, 3.0%); Bank of Canada business survey; NAHB index (31, 32) | Steel Dynamics, Zions, Fifth Third, Western Alliance |
| Tue Oct 20 | China loan prime rates (3.0% and 3.5%, hold expected); US housing starts (1.30m, 1.275m) and permits (1.40m, 1.403m); pending home sales (−0.4% m/m, +0.3%); UK unemployment (5.0%, 4.9%); German ZEW (31.6, 34.7) | General Motors, RTX, Netflix, GE Aerospace, Capital One, Northrop Grumman, United Airlines, 3M, KeyCorp |
| Wed Oct 21 | UK CPI (3.4%, 3.1%); EIA crude stocks (prior −8.6m barrels); 20-year bond auction (5.42% prior); Lagarde and Bailey speak | **Meta**, **Tesla**, Elevance Health, AT&T, IBM, Lam Research, Texas Instruments, Thermo Fisher |
| Thu Oct 22 | Jobless claims (200k, 199k); leading index (−0.2%, −0.1%); euro area consumer confidence (−16.0, −16.5); 5-year TIPS auction (1.955% prior); Japan CPI after the US close (2.3%, 1.9%) | Procter & Gamble, Comcast, Lockheed Martin, Union Pacific, Valero, Honeywell, Newmont, Huntington |
| Fri Oct 23 | Flash PMIs: US composite (57.6, 58.4), euro area (52.3, 53.1), Germany (53.0, 53.8), UK (51.7, 52.0); UK retail sales (−0.2% m/m, +0.5%); Canada retail sales | American Express, SLB |

Consensus and prior from FMP's calendars; 76 S&P 500 companies report this week.

### What we're watching, by market

- **US equities:** the model's equity calls get a live test. Regional banks are its top preference and Zions, Fifth Third, KeyCorp and Huntington report. Aerospace and defense is an avoid, and RTX, Northrop and Lockheed all report. Last week's breadth (equal weight up, cap weight down) is the trade we want to keep owning; we would not chase a Meta bounce in the Nasdaq-100.
- **Rates:** the 2-year at 4.74% sits 74bp above the top of the 3.75%–4.00% funds range, so the market already leans toward tighter policy. The 10-year real yield is 2.78% and the 10-year breakeven 2.35%. That is why the model's largest fixed income tilt is a 7% overweight in TIPS: breakevens look cheap against $99 oil.
- **Credit:** the cracks are in the basement. High-yield spreads widened to 3.23% as of Thursday from 2.70% a month earlier; CCC spreads rose about 200bp to 12.78% over the same span. CCC bonds are down 5.2% this year while BBs are up 0.3% and Bs 1.2%. Stay up in quality.
- **Commodities:** Wednesday's inventory report follows an 8.6-million-barrel draw. Valero and SLB give the industry's view of margins and drilling. Oil and gas E&P, a model preference, trades at its 52-week high.
- **International:** China's GDP print sets the tone for emerging markets after EEM's 5.9% drop last week. The UK, another model preference, releases jobs, CPI and retail sales in four days; a hot CPI would push gilt yields higher and test that call.

### Looking further out

The following week is the heavyweight round:

- **Mon Oct 26 and Tue Oct 27:** 2-year (4.787% prior) and 5-year (5.033% prior) note auctions; durable goods; Conference Board confidence (81.9 prior).
- **Wed Oct 28:** the FOMC decides; consensus is a hold at 3.75%–4.00%. The Bank of Canada decides (2.25%). Microsoft and Alphabet report.
- **Thu Oct 29:** Q3 GDP (3.1% expected, 2.2% prior) and September PCE (core 3.3% y/y expected, 3.0% prior); the ECB decides (deposit rate 2.50%); 7-year auction; Amazon, Eli Lilly, Caterpillar and Intel report.
- **Fri Oct 30:** the Bank of Japan decides (1.25%); employment cost index; euro area Q3 GDP; Exxon and Chevron report. Apple follows on November 2.

### Bottom line

We read last week as a rotation inside a bull market, and we give that view 60% odds. The dashboard agrees in its own way: 67% equities against a 60% neutral, with its favorites in regional banks, oil and gas producers and the UK. Its live record began with the first saved call on October 17; no session has closed since, so there is nothing to score yet. What would change our mind is credit. If high-yield spreads push through 3.50% while Meta trims its spending plan, we would cut equity risk and add to Treasuries and TIPS. Until then, own breadth, own quality credit, and let the megacaps prove themselves.

title: The Generals Retreated, the Troops Held
headline: The S&P 500 fell 2.0% as chips sank 10.5%, but the equal-weighted index rose and bonds rallied: a rotation inside a bull market, with a warning light in CCC credit.
body:
### The week in one paragraph

The S&P 500 fell 2.0% in its worst week since June, but the damage was concentrated. The Nasdaq-100 lost 5.5% and semiconductors 10.5%, while the equal-weighted S&P 500 *rose* 0.5% and Russell 1000 Value gained 0.9%. Consumer staples (+5.0%), energy (+4.9%) and health care (+3.5%) led. This was a rotation, not a rout: the generals retreated while the troops held their ground. Bonds did their job again, with the 10-year Treasury yield down 12bp to 5.10% as stocks slid. The VIX jumped 35% to 20.0, which is elevated but not panicked.

### Scoreboard

| Market | Level | Week | Year to date |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 (SPY) | 763.25 | −2.0% | +12.8% |
| Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) | 709.80 | −5.5% | +15.9% |
| S&P 500 equal weight (RSP) | 214.09 | +0.5% | +13.1% |
| Russell 1000 Value (IWD) | 255.77 | +0.9% | +22.9% |
| Russell 1000 Growth (IWF) | 121.48 | −5.0% | +2.9% |
| Russell 2000 (IWM) | 270.44 | −3.1% | +10.6% |
| Developed ex-US (EFA) | 103.55 | +0.2% | +9.5% |
| Emerging markets (EEM) | 62.85 | −5.9% | +15.5% |
| 10-year Treasury | 5.10% | −12bp | +92bp |
| High yield (HYG) | 76.86 | −0.5% | −0.3% |
| WTI crude | $99.02 | +7.8% | +72.5% |
| Gold | $4,181 | −0.8% | −3.7% |
| Dollar index | 101.66 | −0.4% | +3.7% |

### Chips down, staples up

The AI complex finally ran into the law of high expectations. ASML beat consensus EPS by 19% and TSMC by 3%, yet SMH dropped 10.5% and technology 7.7%. When beats get sold, the bar has moved above what even excellent results can clear. Korea, the market's purest memory-chip play, fell 15.1%.

We don't read this as the end of the AI cycle. Capex intentions on earnings calls are still rising, and AI and data centers came up on 81% of S&P 500 calls last season, against 69% a year earlier. What it does tell us is that leadership is broadening. The equal-weighted index beat the cap-weighted one by about 2.5 points in a single week. That's healthy for the bull market and painful for anyone overweight the top ten.

### Inflation: hot at the pump, cool underneath

- **Consumer prices:** September CPI rose 0.6% m/m and 3.7% y/y, as oil near $100 worked through. Core CPI rose 0.3% m/m and 2.6% y/y, which is not alarming.
- **Pipeline:** producer prices were the hot spot, up 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, with core PPI up 0.7%. Import prices rose 1.1% m/m.
- **What bonds believe:** the 10-year breakeven is 2.35%, up only 7bp over the past year even as crude has roughly doubled. The market is treating the energy shock as a level shift, not a new inflation regime.
- **Who did the tightening:** the 10-year TIPS real yield rose 102bp over the year to 2.78%. Real rates are doing the Fed's work.

### Growth: no recession in these numbers

Headline retail sales rose just 0.1%, but sales ex-autos rose 0.9% and the year-on-year pace is 6.3% nominal. Industrial production jumped 0.7%, the Empire State survey surged to 25.5 (10.3 expected), and jobless claims held at 199,000. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow puts Q3 at 3.6%. The Philly Fed's slide to 20.9 from 37.8, with new orders down to 4.3, is the one soft spot worth watching.

### The Fed: Warsh keeps his options open

The Fed raised rates to 3.75%–4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023, and the median dot shows one more in December. This week Chair Warsh declined to pre-commit, and traders scaled back bets on an October hike. With core CPI at 2.6% and real yields near 2.8%, the case for a second hike is weaker than the September dots suggested. The FOMC announces its decision on October 28.

### Credit: watch the bottom of the stack

Investment grade spreads barely moved, at 84bp. High yield widened 8bp on the week and 47bp over the month to 323bp. CCC spreads blew out 193bp in a month to 1,278bp, within a few basis points of their widest in three years. The weakest borrowers are feeling 5% Treasury yields first. Year to date, CCCs are down 5.2% while BBs are up 0.3%. That divergence is our main risk flag.

### Earnings season: off to a strong start

Financials set a high bar:

- **Beats:** Goldman Sachs (EPS $17.01 vs $12.86 expected), BlackRock (+11%), Citigroup (+7%), Morgan Stanley (+3%), UnitedHealth (+13%), Johnson & Johnson (+3%).
- **Misses:** JPMorgan (−3%) and Bank of America (−2%), both modest.

The season's first 31 S&P 500 calls are running more upbeat than a year ago. Last season, 25% of companies mentioned raising guidance against 17% a year earlier.

### What the model says

The dashboard's allocation models still favor equities modestly: 67% against a 60% neutral, up from 66% a month ago. In fixed income they overweight TIPS and EM local-currency bonds against the Agg. In equities they prefer:

- **Regional banks:** 1.2× book value.
- **Oil & gas E&P:** at its 52-week high.
- **The UK:** 5.7% shareholder yield.
- **Global ex-US:** 11.3× forward earnings.

They avoid metals & mining, aerospace & defense and consumer discretionary. This week's rotation went the model's way.

### Bottom line

Our read is a rotation within a bull market, not the start of a bear market. Earnings are strong, the economy is running near 3.5% real growth, and long-run inflation expectations are anchored. The risks are 5% long yields, $100 oil and a CCC market that is cracking. We would use AI weakness to rebalance toward the broader market rather than to chase it lower, and keep a close eye on high yield.
